messages.subject: [statnet_help] Courses on "Inferential Network Analysis" and "Discourse Network Analysis"
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Courses on "Inferential Network Analysis" and "Discourse Network Analysis"
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I will offer two courses on network analysis at the ECPR Winter School
in March 2018:

1. Introduction to Discourse Network Analysis (DNA) - 2-3 March 2018

2. Inferential Network Analysis - 5-9 March 2018

The first course introduces a combination of qualitative content
analysis and social network analysis using the software Discourse
Network Analyzer. More information:
https://ecpr.eu/Events/PanelDetails.aspx?PanelID=7452&EventID=120

The second course focuses on exponential random graph models (ERGM) and
also covers related statistical techniques for network data, such as the
(temporal) network autocorrelation model, the TERGM, relational event
models, and several other models. The course both contains theoretical
sessions and applied computer lab sessions using R. More information:
https://ecpr.eu/Events/PanelDetails.aspx?PanelID=7418&EventID=120

The ECPR Winter School is one of the two training opportunities offered
by the European Consortium for Political Research. It takes place in
Bamberg (Germany). Registration is open now. Attendants from ECPR member
institutions can get an early registration discount until 3 November.
More information and registration:
https://ecpr.eu/Events/EventDetails.aspx?EventID=120

Best regards

Philip

--
Dr Philip Leifeld
Senior Lecturer (Associate Professor) in Research Methods
Director of Graduate Training
School of Social and Political Sciences
University of Glasgow
http://www.philipleifeld.com

[University of Glasgow: The Times Scottish University of the Year 2018]

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users,


I work on (ethnic) homophily in social networks. An hypothesis I want to test is whether the ties that are embedded in higher level structures are more homophilic, on average, than the ones who are not.


>From my original network, I can extract only those edges that are reciprocated (ie, symmetrizing the network); then that are part of a full triad ; that are part of a clique of size 4, 5 and so on. In each case, I am interested in comparing the levels of homophily ("nodematch" term) among the edges of the subset with that of the whole network.


How can I do this using ERGMs ? Extracting a subset of my network  and estimating an ERGM model with the "nodematch" term for that subset is pretty easy, but how to make sure that the increase in homophily that I may observe in the new subset is not a mechanical result produced by the extraction itself ? For e.g., I guess that if you symmetrize a random network, the homophily rates observed in the symmetrized graph will always be higher than that of the original graph. Is there a way to assess the statistical significance of the increase in homophily that I observe in symmetrical links ?


Below is an example using statnet built-in data. I only show it for reciprocal as opposed to all links, but I ask myself the same question about links within triads or cliques.

library(statnet)
library(stargazer)

data("faux.dixon.high")
net <- faux.dixon.high

net.s <- as.sociomatrix(net)
net.s <- symmetrize(net.s, rule = "strong")
net.s <- network(net.s,directed = F)

net.s%v%"race" <- as.character(net%v%"race")

m1 <- ergm(net ~ edges + nodematch('race'))
s1 <- ergm(net.s ~ edges + nodematch('race'))

stargazer(m1,s1,type="text")

# The nodematch coefficient is greater ! Does it mean reciprocal ties are more often homophilic ?

summary(net ~ edges + nodematch('race'))
summary(net.s ~ edges + nodematch('race'))

912/1197
180/219

# There is indeed a greater proportion of symmetric ties that are homophilic. But is it significant ?

At some point I thought that it may be done using interaction effects (modelling the interaction effect between the "mutual" and "nodematch" term in an ERGM model applied to the full network) but I don't know whether the ERGM package can do this. Do you have any ideas or suggestions on how to work around that problem ?


Many thanks for the help !


Best Regards


---------------------------------

Timoth?e Chabot

PhD Researcher

European University Institute

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error in MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,


I have a notwork of 84 nodes, undirected.  Ten members of the network were absent at the day of data collection. I estimate a model with edeges and triangle (R 3.4.2; statnet 2016.9).

Yet, it brings error:


> helpmodel.02 <- ergm(schoolhelp~edges+triangle)
Starting maximum likelihood estimation via MCMLE:
Iteration 1 of at most 20:
Optimizing with step length 0.000369932771454251.
The log-likelihood improved by 0.09642.
Iteration 2 of at most 20:
Error in ergm.MCMLE(init, nw, model, initialfit = (initialfit <- NULL),  :
  Unconstrained MCMC sampling did not mix at all. Optimization cannot continue.

Here is the basic info of the network:
 vertices = 84
  directed = FALSE
  hyper = FALSE
  loops = FALSE
  multiple = FALSE
  bipartite = FALSE
 total edges = 1208
   missing edges = 805
   non-missing edges = 403
 density = 0.1156053

And here is the null model:
Formula:   schoolhelp ~ edges
Iterations:  5 out of 20
Monte Carlo MLE Results:
      Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value
edges -1.73212    0.05404      0  <1e-04 ***?
Signif. codes:  0 ?***? 0.001 ?**? 0.01 ?*? 0.05 ?.? 0.1 ? ? 1
     Null Deviance: 3717  on 2681  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 2270  on 2680  degrees of freedom
AIC: 2272    BIC: 2277    (Smaller is better.)

Anyone has ideas how to tackle the problem? Thank you.

Best,
Shupin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error in MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Shupin,

The edges+triangle model is well known in the field for being a 
"degenerate" model specification.  There is a substantial literature on 
the problem of degeneracy in specifying models for ERGs -- it's not a 
problem with the method, it is a problem of model specification. 
Essentially, this result means "that model would never have produced 
the network you observe"

Try using the gwesp terms instead. And if you're not familiar with them I 
suggest you take a look at the following papers:

Snijders TAB, Pattison PE, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New 
specifications for exponential random graph models. In: Stolzenberg RM, 
editor. Sociological Methodology 2006, Vol 362006. p. 99-153.

Hunter DR. Curved Exponential Family Models for Social Networks. 
Social networks. 2007;29(2):216-30. doi: 10.1016/j.socnet.2006.08.005. 
PubMed PMID: PMC2031865.



best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 答复: Error in MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Shupin -

If you are using gwesp() and still having issues, this can suggest that 
you are trying to model clustering associated with an underlying source 
of heterogeneity (e.g., homophily or propinquity on unobserved 
variables) with a homogeneous mechanism (here, the ESP effects that go 
into the GWESP term).? Adding more covariate effects, or looking more 
carefully at how they are parameterized, can often make a huge 
difference.? (In essence, the issue is that GWESP and friends are trying 
to capture the pattern of triadic closure by positing a uniform tendency 
towards closure that affects the entire network equally.? If what is 
really going on is that your clustering is the result of some 
inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the Scylla of not 
producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of the graph 
and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the low-density 
portions of the graph.? The way the model resolves this untenable 
situation is not always to one's liking.)

Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal 
effect of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.? 
But I would start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and 
asking whether it is plausible that you are leaving out some important 
sources of heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about 
homogeneous sources of dependence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

into the GWESP term).  Adding more covariate effects, or looking more
carefully at how they are parameterized, can often make a huge
difference.  (In essence, the issue is that GWESP and friends are trying
to capture the pattern of triadic closure by positing a uniform tendency
towards closure that affects the entire network equally.  If what is
really going on is that your clustering is the result of some
inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the Scylla of not
producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of the graph
and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the low-density
portions of the graph.  The way the model resolves this untenable
situation is not always to one's liking.)

Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal
effect of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.
But I would start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and
asking whether it is plausible that you are leaving out some important
sources of heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about
homogeneous sources of dependence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error term in ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I?m using ERGM to model injection drug user network, and I?m trying to select terms for the formation/dissolution formulas.

Generally speaking, should we put all the important terms into the formula to try to get a best representation of the network, or should we only include those we are interested in (e.g. some variable related to intervention we will simulate)? If we only include the terms we are interested in, is there an error term in the model to catch the residuals? I assume there is, but haven?t seen much about it, are there any resources on this?

In addition, if we have a term (e.g. homophily in something) that drives the formation hugely, but we leave out the term because we won?t use it for disease transmission/intervention later, what consequences it can have? Or it doesn?t matter?

Thank you.

Best,
Lin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error term in ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lin,

> Generally speaking, should we put all the important terms into the formula to try to get a best representation of the network, or should we only include those we are interested in (e.g. some variable related to intervention we will simulate)? If we only include the terms we are interested in, is there an error term in the model to catch the residuals? I assume there is, but haven?t seen much about it, are there any resources on this?

About the "error term" issue:  there are no residuals in the usual
sense (fitted Y - observed Y) in ERGM nor a single numerical index
like R-squared. The main way to asses goodness of fit of an ERGM is to
simulate a lot of networks from the fitted model and compare
(distributions of) their features to the features of the observed
network. For example you can compare the observed degree distribution
to the degree distributions of the generated networks. See e.g.
section 7 of https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v024i03 and
http://stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/tr0502.pdf .


> In addition, if we have a term (e.g. homophily in something) that drives the formation hugely, but we leave out the term because we won?t use it for disease transmission/intervention later, what consequences it can have? Or it doesn?t matter?

As to the more general issue of model specification: it is hard to say
not knowing the details of your research questions and study design.
My vague intuition is that you will probably want to estimate a good
model for your data (all necessary terms) and then use it to evaluate
your possible interventions. I'm not sure why one would want to omit
terms that are clearly relevant for the network structure, even though
they are not your "intervention variables".


Best,
Michal

Only thing I would add is that lowering alpha towards gwesp(0) becomes 
problematic in dense networks, where every edge is likely to be involved 
in at least one triangle (thx to Steve Goodreau for reminding me of this 
yesterday).

suggest looking at summary(netw ~ edges + gwesp(0, fixed=T) + ...) to 
see whether the summary statistics for the gwesp(0) term is almost equal 
to the number of dyads.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error term in ERGM
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 16 Nov 2017, Zhu, Lin wrote:

> Generally speaking, should we put all the important terms into the formula to try to get a best representation of the
> network, or should we only include those we are interested in (e.g. some variable related to intervention we will
> simulate)? If we only include the terms we are interested in, is there an error term in the model to catch the residuals?
> I assume there is, but haven?t seen much about it, are there any resources on this?

Since Michal responded to this, I won't say much more.  Just that this is 
a statistical model, so it does have a predicted and an error component. 
But it is a generalized linear model, so the relationship between the 
observed data (0 or 1) and the predicted value (the odds of a tie) is a 
bit more complicated.  Think logistic regression.

> In addition, if we have a term (e.g. homophily in something) that drives the formation hugely, but we leave out the term
> because we won?t use it for disease transmission/intervention later, what consequences it can have? Or it doesn?t matter?

If this term is a highly significant driver of formation (and possibly 
dissolution), and you leave it out, the networks you simulate from your 
model will not look like the network you observe in the data.  We know 
that homophily has a strong impact on diffusion processes in networks, so 
we can also say with some confidence that your diffusion model will also 
not represent what would happen in the true network.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM Convergence Statistics (t-ratio) using R-package 3.4.2
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Members,

I have question about reporting the goodness of fit statistics of an ERGM
model in a paper, such as p-value or t-ratio. I have read few papers (e.g.
Brailly, 2016; Lee and Lee, 2014) that have reported convergence statistics
as t-ratio in order to show the goodness of fit of the models.

Here, I have two questions.

Q1. Can we report p-values as convergence statistics to show the goodness
of fit of our model?

Q2. If the answer to my first question is No, can we use R-package to
calculate the t-ratio to show the goodness of fit of our model. I was
wondering whether it is possible to calculate the t-ratios in R-package and
I am not aware of that. Any suggestion will be highly appreciated.

As far as I know, t-ratio can be calculated by using P-Net software and the
R package calculates p-values (but, not t-ratio) for the goodness of fit
statistics by using the following command;

summary(network.model.gof)


Reference:

Brailly, J. (2016). "Dynamics of networks in trade fairs?A multilevel
relational approach to the cooperation among competitors." *Journal of
Economic Geography* *16*(6): 1279-1301.

Lee, S. and C. Lee (2014). "Creative Interaction and Multiplexity in
Intraorganizational Networks." *Management Communication Quarterly* *29*(1):
56-83.
I will be grateful for any help.


Thank you and regards,

Owais A. Golra, MSc (Res), BSc (Engg.)
